{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "B shows money already flowing into its category, even if not from end users. BikeMaps.org got $930,000 in government grants, Pointz raised $520k, and advocacy nonprofits like the League of American Bicyclists collect $50/yr dues while running similar tools. A shows no money flowing into Pascal documentation at all, and notes that the Foundation funds development, not docs.",
    "B names institutional buyers a solo operator could approach directly within 90 days: advocacy nonprofits, municipal Vision Zero programs and research grants. A's only payer is hypothetical: unnamed 'companies shipping commercial Lazarus-based products,' with no example or source.",
    "A's own case against says the real blocker may be maintainers unwilling to engage with doc fixes, not tooling. An outside product cannot fix that. It also says the developer population looks too small to sustain revenue. Those points weaken A's core premise, not just its pricing.",
    "A's demand evidence is partly old (a 2010 mailing-list post and a Reddit thread from around the Lazarus 1.2 release). It shows frustration, not willingness to pay. B's demand evidence is also soft, but it comes with several live, operating products that prove the function is wanted.",
    "B carries real costs A does not: liability, moderation and seeding data in a new city. The brief at least names these and offers bounded fixes (one-time legal consult, privacy review, waiver). A's main risks, no payer and a tiny market, have no such fix."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's payer claim that 'companies shipping commercial Lazarus-based products' might pay for a hosted or high-SLA docs tier. No such company is named or sourced. The ~$50/month price is borrowed from Read the Docs Business pricing, not drawn from any Pascal user, while every competitor in A's space is free.",
  "confidence_note": "Low-to-moderate confidence. Neither brief shows a single paying customer or a validated price, and both rely on frustration quotes rather than willingness-to-pay evidence. B wins mainly because its category shows institutional money and reachable organizational buyers, while A shows no payer and admits its bottleneck may not be solvable by tooling. B's liability and cold-start data problems could still sink a 90-day timeline."
}
